claim: Station HYPO under Commander Joseph Rochefort read the Japanese plan and the date; a PBY sighted the Japanese carriers at about 05:30 on 4 June 1942
source: Wikipedia, Battle of Midway; Naval History and Heritage Command, Midway overview
note: The 05:34 report time and the 07:02 launch time on the report are modeled to the standard timelines; the screen shows them as dispatch times, not as quotations.

claim: Torpedo Eight lost all fifteen aircraft and all but one of its crews; the torpedo squadrons scored no hit and drew the Japanese fighters low before the dive bombers arrived at about 10:22
source: Wikipedia, Battle of Midway; Wikipedia, Torpedo Squadron 8
note: Torpedo Six and Torpedo Three losses given as 'most of theirs'; exact counts not opened.

claim: Akagi, Kaga and Soryu were put out of action in about five minutes by the Enterprise and Yorktown dive bombers; Hiryu hit Yorktown twice that afternoon and was sunk in the evening; Hornet's air group missed the enemy
note: The Japanese-side detail comes from Parshall and Tully (Shattered Sword) via the secondary summary; the book itself was not opened.

claim: Nimitz's order to the carriers was the principle of calculated risk (not to be exposed to superior force without a good prospect of damaging the enemy)
source: Wikipedia, Battle of Midway (citing Nimitz's operation plan)
note: The hard-mode rule in the game paraphrases this; it is not given as a quotation.

claim: The Naval Battle of Guadalcanal ran from 12 to 15 November 1942; Rear Admirals Callaghan and Scott were killed, the only two US flag officers killed in a surface action in the war; Japan lost two battleships, one heavy cruiser, three destroyers, eleven transports and 64 aircraft
source: Naval History and Heritage Command, Naval Battle of Guadalcanal; Wikipedia, Naval Battle of Guadalcanal

claim: Tanaka's convoy of eleven transports carried about 7,000 troops; seven transports were sunk by aircraft on 14 November, four were beached on 15 November; about 2,000 troops were landed
source: Wikipedia, Naval Battle of Guadalcanal; Wikipedia, Raizo Tanaka; Naval History and Heritage Command
note: Sources give the landed troops as about 2,000 to 3,000; the game says about 2,000.

claim: Washington sank Kirishima by radar-directed fire on the night of 14 to 15 November at about 8,500 yards; Suzuya and Maya shelled Henderson Field for about 35 minutes after midnight on 14 November; Kinugasa was sunk by American aircraft the next morning
source: Wikipedia, Naval Battle of Guadalcanal; DANFS, USS Washington (BB-56); Wikipedia, Henderson Field

claim: Vice Admiral Jinichi Kusaka commanded the Southeast Area Fleet at Rabaul; Rabaul is about 560 miles from Guadalcanal
source: From memory of the standard histories
note: To be checked against a primary source before release.

claim: Albacore sank Taiho and Cavalla sank Shokaku on 19 June 1944; Flying Fish sighted the Japanese fleet on 15 June and Seahorse tracked it on the 16th
source: National Park Service, Battle of the Philippine Sea; Wikipedia, Battle of the Philippine Sea
note: The Flying Fish and Seahorse dates come from the secondary summary only.

claim: Japan lost an estimated 550 to 645 aircraft in the battle against about 123 American; about 80 American aircraft were lost on the dark return of 20 June; Mitscher ordered the ships' lights turned on
source: EBSCO Research Starters, Battle of the Philippine Sea; Wikipedia, Battle of the Philippine Sea; USS Boston (CA-69) association account of 20 June 1944
note: Counts differ by source; the game gives the range and 'about'.

claim: Mitscher launched his strike late on 20 June at long range after a search plane found the Japanese carriers at 1615 and more than 200 miles away; Hiyo was sunk
source: Encyclopedia.com, Philippine Sea, Battle of the; the vf31.com squadron account
note: Range and launch time differ by account; the game says 'long range' and 'more than two hundred miles'.

claim: Task Group 58.7 under Vice Admiral Willis Lee formed the battle line west of the carriers on 19 June; Vice Admiral Charles Lockwood commanded the Pacific Fleet submarines; Vice Admiral William Calhoun commanded the Service Force, Pacific Fleet
source: From memory of the standard histories
note: To be checked against a primary source before release.
